newsitem.title: USA: VOA to launch new Serbian-language TV show.
newsitem.headline: VOA to launch new Serbian-language TV show.

text.p: The Voice of America, in another response to the political crisis in Serbia, on Wednesday announced plans to begin broadcasting a daily half-hour Serbian language television programme.
The programme, entitled "America Calling Serbia," will air five days a weeks on its WORLDNET network and be broadcast simultaneously on radio and television.
"This VOA initiative to simulcast television and radio programming is an historic breakthrough," David Burke, chairman of the broadcasting board of governors, said in a statement.

"By using radio, TV and the Internet, VOA expands its delivery of accurate, objective information to the people of Serbia. This is another exmaple of how international broadcasters can and do fill a vital information void in today's volatile post-Cold War world," he said.
VOA last week expanded its Serbian language radio broadcasts after Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic shut down the main independent radio station B92.

After pressure from the United States and other countries, B92 was allowed to resume broadcasting. VOA said it would continue to broadcast two hours of Serbian-language radio a day, in addition to 30 minutes of Bosnian, 90 minutes of Croatian and 40 minutes of Slovene to the former Yugoslavia.

On the new television programme, the VOA statement said it would broadcast throughout Serbia and include 10-minute news reports, conferences, U.S. reactions to events and stringer and correspondent reports from around the world.
There are nearly 500,000 satellite dishes in Serbia, the VOA said.
The VOA said it broadcasts international, regional and U.S. news in 52 languages to en estimated weekly audience of 86 million listeners.
Huge anti-government protest marches began in Serbia after President Milosevic's socialist government annulled opposition victories in local elections 25 days ago.

The Yugoslav opposition on Wednesday was pinning its hopes on union backing and growing international support in its battle for control of town councils amid signs that support for its rallies is starting to fade.
